title: EMR — Experience Modification Rate
applicability: A workers' compensation premium multiplier assigned to any employer whose payroll/premium exceeds the state eligibility threshold. Compares an employer's ACTUAL losses to EXPECTED losses for its class codes over a 3-year experience period (lagged ~1 year, most recent policy year excluded). 1.00 = industry-average; below 1.00 = credit (safer than peers), above 1.00 = debit. Rated by NCCI in ~35+ states; independent bureaus rate the rest (e.g., California/WCIRB, New York/NYCIRB, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, Wisconsin, and monopolistic states OH/ND/WA/WY).
required_elements: Payroll by class code for the 3-year experience period
Expected Loss Rate (ELR) per $100 payroll, published by the rating bureau per class code
D-Ratio (discount ratio) per class code — splits expected losses into primary vs. excess
Split point — the per-claim dollar cap dividing each claim into primary (capped, full weight) and excess (dampened) loss
Actual incurred losses, split into primary and excess (medical-only claims reduced to 30% of primary)
Weighting value (W) and Ballast value (B) from the bureau credibility tables, based on total expected losses
failure_points: Payroll misclassified to a higher-hazard class code, inflating expected losses
Open/reserved claims carried at inflated reserves not reviewed before unit-stat filing
Failing to dispute unit statistical data errors within the correction window
Claim frequency (many small claims) — hurts more than one large claim because primary losses carry full weight
Submitting an EMR without the matching rating-bureau worksheet when a hiring client asks for verification
notes: EMR is calculated by the rating bureau/carrier, not self-reported — but contractors must UNDERSTAND it to (a) reduce it and (b) explain an elevated mod to a hiring client. Reduction levers: aggressive return-to-work/light-duty (converts lost-time claims to medical-only), claims management and reserve review, safety program that cuts FREQUENCY, and auditing payroll class codes. The single most impactful because frequency drives primary losses.
formula:
Mod = ( Ap + W·Ae + B ) / ( Ep + W·Ee + B )
  Ap = actual primary losses (capped at split point)
  Ae = actual excess losses (above split point)
  Ep = expected primary losses (= expected losses × D-ratio)
  Ee = expected excess losses (= expected losses − expected primary)
  W  = weighting value (rises with employer size)
  B  = ballast value (stabilizes toward 1.00)
Expected losses by class = (Payroll ÷ 100) × ELR, summed across all class codes.
NCCI's simplified/split-plan form (post-2017): Mod ≈ ( Ap + Ee ) ÷ E, where the primary/excess weighting is pre-built into the bureau's limited rating factors.
calc_example: Employer with $200,000 expected losses; $88,100 actual primary and $75,640 actual excess (total actual $163,740); W = 0.16, B = $45,900. Plug primary at full weight and excess at the weighted rate into the formula → a mod near or below 1.00 yields a premium credit. A $100,000 manual premium × EMR 0.85 = $85,000 (saves $15,000/yr); × EMR 1.30 = $130,000.
benchmarks: 1.00 = industry average. Many oil & gas / construction operators require EMR < 1.00 to bid; some petrochemical owners cut off at 1.0 hard, others allow up to ~1.25 with a corrective plan. Below 0.80 is considered excellent. EMR is one of the three stats (with TRIR and DART) that prequalification platforms score.

title: TRIR — Total Recordable Incident Rate
applicability: The headline OSHA rate: all recordable injuries and illnesses per 100 full-time-equivalent workers per year. Used by every prequalification platform and most GCs as a first-pass safety screen. Computed from the OSHA 300 log and total hours worked.
required_elements: Count of OSHA-recordable cases (any case meeting 1904.7: death, days away, restricted/transfer, medical treatment beyond first aid, loss of consciousness, or significant diagnosis)
Total hours actually worked by all employees in the period (do NOT use 2,000×headcount if actual hours are available; exclude vacation/leave)
200,000-hour base constant (100 employees × 40 hrs × 50 weeks)
failure_points: Using scheduled hours instead of hours actually worked
Counting first-aid-only cases as recordable (over-counting) OR omitting recordable restricted-duty cases (under-counting)
Rate that doesn't reconcile to the submitted OSHA 300A totals
Three-year trend inconsistent with the 300A logs on file
notes: TRIR is self-reported but must tie exactly to the OSHA 300A logs the contractor uploads. Platforms score the 3-year TRIR against the NAICS benchmark; a rate above the industry average with no improvement trend is a common grade downgrade.
formula: TRIR = ( Number of OSHA-recordable cases × 200,000 ) ÷ Total hours worked
calc_example: 8 recordable cases over 430,000 hours worked → (8 × 200,000) ÷ 430,000 = 3.72 TRIR.
benchmarks: BLS Survey of Occupational Injuries & Illnesses (SOII), 2024 data (released Jan 2026): all private industry ≈ 2.3–2.7; Construction (NAICS 23) ≈ 2.3–2.5; Oil & gas extraction (NAICS 211) ≈ 0.8–1.4; Support activities for O&G (213112) ≈ 1.6; Manufacturing ≈ 2.8–3.2; Transportation & warehousing ≈ 4.0–4.8. Rates update annually — always pull the CURRENT BLS figure for the contractor's specific NAICS. Many GCs set a hard bid cutoff of TRIR < 1.0–2.0.

title: DART — Days Away, Restricted, or Transferred Rate
applicability: A severity-weighted rate: only the more serious cases — those resulting in days away from work, restricted duty, or job transfer — per 100 FTE. Always ≤ TRIR (it is a subset). Distinguishes serious injuries from minor medical-treatment cases.
required_elements: Count of DART cases (cases with days away, restricted work, or job transfer per the 300 log columns)
Total hours worked
200,000 base constant
failure_points: Confusing DART with DAFW/LTIR — DART includes restricted/transfer, lost-time (DAFW) does not
Not classifying a restricted-duty case as DART because 'no days were lost'
DART higher than TRIR (impossible — a data error)
notes: Return-to-work / light-duty programs are the primary DART lever: keeping an injured worker on restricted duty still counts as a DART case, but converting a would-be lost-time case to medical-only keeps it OUT of DART. This is also why aggressive RTW lowers EMR.
formula: DART = ( Number of DART cases × 200,000 ) ÷ Total hours worked
benchmarks: BLS SOII 2024: all private industry DART ≈ 1.4–1.5; Construction ≈ 1.5; Oil & gas extraction ≈ 0.4–0.9; Manufacturing ≈ 1.6–1.8. DART is roughly 55–65% of TRIR in most industries.

title: DAFW / LTIR — Days Away From Work (Lost Time) Rate
applicability: The narrowest severity rate: only cases with actual days away from work (lost-time), per 100 FTE. Sometimes labeled LTIR (Lost Time Incident Rate) or LTC rate. Excludes restricted-duty and transfer-only cases (which DART includes).
required_elements: Count of days-away cases (300 log column H)
Total hours worked
200,000 base constant
failure_points: Using DAFW and DART interchangeably
Excluding cases that had days away AND restricted days (still a DAFW case)
formula: DAFW/LTIR = ( Number of days-away cases × 200,000 ) ÷ Total hours worked
benchmarks: BLS SOII 2024: all private industry DAFW ≈ 0.8–0.9. Reported on the 300A as the 'cases with days away from work' column.

title: Severity Rate (Lost Workday Rate)
applicability: Measures how SERIOUS injuries are, not how often they occur: total lost/restricted days per 100 FTE. A company can have a low TRIR but a high severity rate if its few injuries are catastrophic. Not an OSHA-defined rate but widely required by owners.
required_elements: Total number of lost (and often restricted) workdays across all cases
Total hours worked
200,000 base constant
failure_points: Capping days at 180 for the rate when the client wants actual days (OSHA caps the 300-log count at 180 per case; confirm which the client wants)
Mixing lost days and restricted days without stating which are included
formula: Severity Rate = ( Total lost workdays × 200,000 ) ÷ Total hours worked

title: Fatality Rate & OSHA Reporting Triggers
applicability: Fatalities are reported to OSHA directly (not just logged) and, for benchmarking, expressed per 100,000 FTE from the BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries (CFOI). Critical because fatality/severe-injury reporting failures are their own citation and a prequalification red flag.
required_elements: Report any work-related fatality to OSHA within 8 hours
Report any in-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye within 24 hours
Report by phone (1-800-321-OSHA), the nearest area office, or the online reporting form
Log the fatality on the OSHA 300 and retain the incident investigation
failure_points: Missing the 8-hour fatality / 24-hour hospitalization-amputation-eye reporting window
Reporting to the wrong channel or not documenting the report
No incident investigation on file to accompany the report
notes: Even one late severe-injury report can trigger an inspection and damage a prequalification score. The 8-hour / 24-hour rule is a frequent audit question.
formula:
Fatality Rate = ( Number of fatalities × 200,000 ) ÷ Total hours worked  (per-100-FTE basis)
BLS CFOI reports fatal injuries per 100,000 full-time-equivalent workers.
benchmarks: BLS CFOI: all-worker fatal injury rate ≈ 3.5 per 100,000 FTE; Construction ≈ 9.6; Oil & gas / mining ≈ 5–11; Agriculture ≈ 18–20; Transportation ≈ 13–14.

title: Certificate of Insurance (COI) — ACORD 25
applicability: The industry-standard one-page proof-of-insurance form. It EVIDENCES coverage but confers no rights and does not amend the policy — the actual risk transfer lives in the policy endorsements, not the certificate. Hiring clients and prequalification platforms collect the ACORD 25 plus the underlying endorsement pages to verify a contractor meets contractual insurance requirements.
required_elements: Producer (insurance agent/broker) and their contact
Named Insured — must exactly match the contracting legal entity (LLC vs. DBA vs. individual)
Insurer(s) affording coverage with NAIC # and A.M. Best rating (clients often require A- VII or better)
Each coverage line with policy number, effective/expiration dates, and limits (see individual coverage entries)
Description of Operations box — names the project and the required contractual wording
Certificate Holder — the hiring client / additional insured requesting the COI
Attached endorsement forms (AI, P&NC, WOS, notice of cancellation) — the COI checkboxes alone are not proof
failure_points: Named Insured on the COI doesn't match the contracting entity
COI shows 'additional insured' checked but the CG 20 10 / CG 20 37 endorsement is not attached
Coverage expired or lapses before the project completion / completed-operations tail
Carrier below the client's required A.M. Best rating
Limits below contract minimums; umbrella not shown as follow-form over GL and Auto
notes: Rule the agent must enforce: 'A certificate without the endorsement is a placeholder — the endorsement is the coverage.' When drafting an insurance-compliance letter, reference the specific ACORD 25 plus the named endorsement forms and edition dates, never just 'we are insured.'

title: Commercial General Liability (CGL)
applicability: Third-party bodily injury and property damage coverage arising from the contractor's operations, products, and completed operations. The core line every hiring client requires. Written on the ISO CG 00 01 occurrence form (preferred over claims-made).
required_elements: Occurrence form (CG 00 01), not claims-made
Typical required limits: $1,000,000 per occurrence / $2,000,000 general aggregate / $2,000,000 products-completed operations aggregate / $1,000,000 personal & advertising injury
Products-Completed Operations coverage maintained through the required tail period
No exclusions that gut the coverage (e.g., action-over/employee-injury exclusion, residential, EIFS, height/exterior) where the work requires it
Aggregate applying per project/per location where required (CG 25 03 / CG 25 04)
failure_points: Limits below the $1M/$2M contract minimum
Claims-made form submitted where occurrence is required
Action-over (employee injury) exclusion present on energy/industrial work
Products-completed operations excluded or expired before the tail runs out
notes: CGL is the policy the AI, P&NC, and WOS endorsements attach to. When a client says 'name us as additional insured, primary & non-contributory, with waiver of subrogation,' they mean on the CGL (and usually Auto and Umbrella too).

title: Workers' Compensation & Employer's Liability
citation: State WC statute + ISO/NCCI WC policy
applicability: Statutory no-fault coverage for employee on-the-job injuries (Part One) plus Employer's Liability (Part Two) for injury claims that fall outside the WC statute. Mandatory in nearly every state for employers; the coverage behind the EMR.
required_elements: Part One — Workers' Compensation: statutory limits per the state(s) of operation
Part Two — Employer's Liability: typical required limits $1,000,000 each accident / $1,000,000 disease-policy limit / $1,000,000 disease-each employee
Correct states listed in Item 3.A. of the Information Page (all states where work is performed)
Waiver of Subrogation endorsement (WC 00 03 13) where the contract requires it
USL&H, Jones Act, or Voluntary Comp endorsements for maritime/offshore energy work where applicable
failure_points: State of operation missing from Item 3.A. (a gap in statutory coverage)
Employer's Liability limits below $1M/$1M/$1M
No WC 00 03 13 waiver of subrogation when required
Ghost/sole-proprietor policy excluding owners where the client requires owner coverage
Missing USL&H/Jones Act on offshore or dock work
notes: Additional-insured status does NOT apply to WC — the risk transfer here is the Waiver of Subrogation (WC 00 03 13). Certificate wording should carve WC out of the AI/P&NC language.

title: Commercial Automobile Liability
applicability: Bodily injury and property damage from owned, hired, and non-owned autos used in the business. Required for any contractor driving to/around a client site or hauling materials/equipment.
required_elements: 'Any Auto' or Owned + Hired + Non-Owned symbols covered
Typical required limit: $1,000,000 combined single limit (CSL)
Additional Insured endorsement (CA 20 48 designated insured) where required
Waiver of subrogation and primary/non-contributory where required
MCS-90 endorsement for DOT-regulated hazmat/interstate motor carriers (see FMCSA category)
failure_points: Hired & non-owned auto not covered though the contractor uses rentals/employee vehicles
Limit below $1M CSL
No MCS-90 where hazmat/interstate hauling requires it
Auto not added to the umbrella's underlying schedule

title: Umbrella / Excess Liability
citation: Follow-Form Umbrella over CGL / Auto / EL
applicability: Extra limits sitting above the CGL, Auto, and Employer's Liability underlying policies. Energy and heavy-industrial owners frequently require substantial umbrella limits on top of the $1M primary.
required_elements: Follow-form over CGL, Commercial Auto, and Employer's Liability (schedule of underlying)
Typical required limits: $1,000,000–$5,000,000+ (energy/petrochemical owners often require $5M–$25M total)
Additional insured and primary/non-contributory following form to the underlying
Drop-down / maintenance-of-underlying terms understood
failure_points: Umbrella not listing the required underlying policies (a coverage gap)
Total limits below the owner's required tower (e.g., $5M required, only $1M shown)
Umbrella not following form for AI/P&NC/WOS

title: Additional Insured Endorsement (AI)
applicability: Extends the contractor's CGL to cover the hiring client/owner as an insured for liability arising out of the contractor's work. Two forms are needed for a construction project's full lifecycle: ongoing operations AND completed operations. This is the single most-commonly-required risk-transfer endorsement.
required_elements: CG 20 10 — Additional Insured, Ongoing Operations (while the contractor is actively working)
CG 20 37 — Additional Insured, Products-Completed Operations (claims after the work is finished)
Schedule naming the client or 'as required by written contract'
Edition date awareness: on 04/13 and later forms, AI limits are the LESSER of the contract-required or the policy limits, and coverage is tied to the named insured's negligence
Blanket AI endorsement acceptable only if it names the party via written-contract trigger
failure_points: Only CG 20 10 provided — leaves completed-operations claims (the biggest construction losses) uncovered
COI shows AI but no endorsement page attached
Endorsement names the wrong legal entity or an expired policy
CG 20 37 references only ongoing operations language (doesn't reach 'your work' in the products-completed operations hazard)
notes: Require BOTH CG 20 10 and CG 20 37 in construction. 'My carrier can't issue CG 20 37' is false — all major carriers issue it, sometimes for a small fee.

title: Primary & Non-Contributory Endorsement (P&NC)
applicability: Makes the contractor's CGL pay FIRST ('primary') and stops the contractor's insurer from demanding the hiring client's own insurer share the loss ('non-contributory'). Paired with AI status so the client's own policy is never touched until the contractor's limits are exhausted.
required_elements: CG 20 01 (04 13 or later) attached to the CGL
Primary and non-contributory language present in the endorsement itself, not merely checked on the COI
Coordinated with the AI endorsement and, where required, on Auto and Umbrella
failure_points: P&NC only referenced on the certificate, not endorsed on the policy
AI granted without P&NC — leaves the client's carrier exposed to a contribution demand
P&NC missing on the umbrella so the tower isn't truly primary

title: Waiver of Subrogation (WOS)
applicability: The contractor's insurer waives its right to recover ('subrogate') from the hiring client after paying a claim. Required separately on the General Liability policy (CG 24 04) and the Workers' Compensation policy (WC 00 03 13) — they are different forms on different policies.
required_elements: CG 24 04 — Waiver of Transfer of Rights of Recovery, on the CGL
WC 00 03 13 — Waiver of Our Right to Recover From Others, on the Workers' Comp policy
Schedule naming the upstream party, or a blanket form triggered by a written waiver requirement
Waiver also on Auto/Umbrella where the contract requires it
failure_points: WC waiver omitted because the party assumed AI/GL waiver covers workers' comp (it does not)
Waiver only checked on the COI, endorsement not attached
Blanket waiver present but the contract required a scheduled (named) waiver

title: Notice of Cancellation Endorsement
applicability: Contractually required advance warning — typically 30 days (10 days for non-payment) — before the insurer cancels or non-renews, so the hiring client isn't blindsided by a lapse. Standard ACORD 25 language now only says notice will be given 'in accordance with the policy provisions,' so an actual endorsement is needed to bind a specific notice period to the certificate holder.
required_elements: Endorsement providing 30 days' advance written notice of cancellation/non-renewal to the certificate holder (10 days for non-payment)
Certificate holder named as the notice recipient
Applies across GL, Auto, WC, and Umbrella as required by contract
failure_points: Relying on the pre-printed ACORD 'endeavor to' language, which binds nothing
No endorsement actually naming the client as notice recipient
Notice period shorter than the contract requires

title: Incident Investigation & Reporting Program
applicability: All contractors. Prequal agencies require a written program governing how injuries, illnesses, near-misses and property-damage events are reported, investigated and closed out.
required_elements: Written procedure requiring prompt reporting of all incidents and near-misses, with no-reprisal language
Investigation methodology that identifies root cause (e.g., 5-Whys, cause tree) rather than only immediate cause
Defined timeline for starting and completing investigations
Corrective/preventive action tracking to closure with assigned owners and due dates
Roles and responsibilities (who reports, who investigates, management review)
OSHA recordkeeping/reporting triggers (fatality within 8 hours; inpatient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye within 24 hours)
Method to communicate lessons learned to the workforce
training: Supervisors and investigators trained in the investigation method and reporting timeline; all employees trained on how and when to report.
recordkeeping: Retain investigation reports, corrective-action logs, and OSHA 300/301 records per 1904 retention (5 years).
failure_points: Program stops at 'immediate cause' with no root-cause analysis
No corrective-action tracking to closure
Missing OSHA 8-hour / 24-hour reporting triggers
No near-miss reporting mechanism
training_verbatim:
(g), (h)(3)(i)
through (iv),
and (j)(3)

(g) Training
(1) Initial training.
(i)

Each employee presently involved in operating a process,
and each employee before being involved in operating a
newly assigned process, shall be trained in an overview of
the process and in the operating procedures as specified
in paragraph (f) of this section. The training shall include
emphasis on the specific safety and health hazards,
emergency operations including shutdown, and safe work
practices applicable to the employee’s job tasks.

(ii) In lieu of initial training for those employees already involved
in operating a process on May 26, 1992, an employer
may certify in writing that the employee has the required
knowledge, skills, and abilities to safely carry out the duties
and responsibilities as specified in the operating procedures.
(2) Refresher training. Refresher training shall be provided at
least every three years, and more often if necessary, to each
employee involved in operating a process to assure that the
employee understands and adheres to the current operating
procedures of the process. The employer, in consultation with the
employees involved in operating the process, shall determine the
appropriate frequency of refresher training.
(3) Training documentation. The employer shall ascertain that
each employee involved in operating a process has received
and understood the training required by this paragraph. The
employer shall prepare a record which contains the identity of
the employee, the date of training, and the means used to verify
that the employee understood the training.

 General Industry

(h) Contractors
(3) Contract employer responsibilities.
(i)

The contract employer shall assure that each contract
employee is trained in the work practices necessary to
perform his/her job.

(ii) The contract employer shall assure that each contract
employee is instructed in the known potential fire,
explosion, or toxic release hazards related to his/her job and
the process, and the applicable provisions of the emergency
action plan.
(iii) The contract employer shall document that each contract
employee has received and understood the training
required by this paragraph. The contract employer shall
prepare a record which contains the identity of the contract
employee, the date of training, and the means used to verify
that the employee understood the training.
(iv) The contract employer shall assure that each contract
employee follows the safety rules of the facility including the
safe work practices required by paragraph (f)(4) of this section.
(j) Mechanical integrity
(3) Training for process maintenance activities. The employer shall
train each employee involved in maintaining the ongoing
integrity of process equipment in an overview of that process and
its hazards and in the procedures applicable to the employee’s job
tasks to assure that the employee can perform the job tasks in a
safe manner.

title: Disciplinary & Enforcement Policy
citation: RAVS-required written program (OSHA General Duty Clause, 29 USC 654(a)(1))
applicability: All contractors. Prequal reviewers require a written, progressive policy showing safety rules are enforced consistently.
required_elements: Written progressive-discipline steps (e.g., verbal, written, suspension, termination) applied to safety-rule violations
Statement that the policy applies to all levels including supervisors and management
Provision for immediate action on willful or life-threatening violations
Consistent, documented application across the workforce
Employee acknowledgement of the policy
training: All employees informed of safety rules and the consequences of violations at orientation.
recordkeeping: Retain signed acknowledgements and disciplinary-action records.
failure_points: Policy exists but excludes supervisors/management
No progressive steps defined
No employee acknowledgement on file

title: Substance Abuse — Drug & Alcohol Program (non-DOT)
citation: RAVS-required written program (client-driven; distinct from 49 CFR Part 40 DOT testing)
applicability: Non-DOT-regulated workers. Most owner clients require a written substance-abuse policy covering the conditions under which testing occurs.
required_elements: Written policy prohibiting drug/alcohol use, possession, and impairment on the job
Testing conditions covered: pre-employment, reasonable suspicion, post-incident, random, return-to-duty
Defined consequences of a positive test and of refusal to test
Chain-of-custody and confidentiality provisions
Compliance with applicable state law and, where workers are safety-sensitive, alignment with DOT 49 CFR Part 40 procedures
Employee Assistance Program (EAP) or referral information where offered
training: Supervisors trained to recognize reasonable-suspicion indicators; employees informed of the policy at hire.
recordkeeping: Retain signed policy acknowledgements and testing records per applicable law; keep DOT and non-DOT records separate.
failure_points: No post-incident or reasonable-suspicion testing defined
Silent on refusal-to-test consequences
Conflicts with state law (e.g., marijuana provisions)

title: Behavior-Based Safety / Safety Observation Program
applicability: Contractors on sites that require a proactive observation/leading-indicator program.
required_elements: Written process for peer safety observations of at-risk vs. safe behaviors
A defined observation card/checklist and how data is collected
Feedback loop: how observations are reviewed and acted on
Tracking of leading indicators and trend review by management
No-blame, coaching-based approach
training: Observers trained on the observation process and giving effective feedback.
recordkeeping: Retain observation records and trend analyses.
failure_points: Data collected but never analyzed or acted on
Used punitively instead of for coaching

title: Management of Change (MOC) Program
applicability: Facilities/operations where changes to process, equipment, chemicals, procedures, or personnel can introduce new hazards. Required under PSM and commonly required by owner clients beyond PSM scope.
required_elements: Written procedure to review changes to technology, equipment, procedures, and organization before implementation
Hazard/technical basis review of the proposed change
Authorization/approval requirements before the change is made
Update of affected process safety information, procedures, and drawings
Communication and training of affected employees and contractors on the change
Distinction between temporary and permanent changes with time limits on temporary changes
training: Employees and contractors affected by a change trained prior to startup.
recordkeeping: Retain MOC review, approval, and close-out records.
failure_points: Only covers equipment, not procedural or organizational change
No pre-startup review or approval step
Temporary changes never closed out

title: Contractor / Subcontractor Safety Management Program
applicability: Contractors that hire lower-tier subcontractors, and host employers evaluating contractors.
required_elements: Written process to pre-qualify subcontractors on safety performance (EMR, TRIR, programs)
Communication of site hazards and rules to subcontractors
Verification of subcontractor training and insurance
Oversight/auditing of subcontractor work and enforcement of safety rules
Evaluation of subcontractor performance and re-qualification
training: Subcontractor employees receive site-specific orientation before starting work.
recordkeeping: Retain prequalification records, orientation rosters, and performance evaluations.
failure_points: No documented prequalification criteria
No verification of sub training/insurance
No performance evaluation loop

title: New Employee Safety Orientation & Training Program
citation: 29 CFR 1910 Subpart-wide training duties + RAVS-required written program
applicability: All contractors. Prequal reviewers require a documented orientation covering hazards and programs before work begins.
required_elements: Written orientation curriculum covering company safety rules, hazard communication, PPE, emergency procedures, and incident reporting
Site-specific hazard orientation for each new location
Documentation of completion (signed roster/acknowledgement) before the employee starts work
Competency verification appropriate to the job
Refresher/annual training schedule
training: This program IS the training baseline; identifies who delivers it and how competency is confirmed.
recordkeeping: Retain signed orientation records and a training matrix by employee and topic.
failure_points: No proof of completion before work starts
Generic only, with no site-specific component
No training matrix showing who is trained on what
training_verbatim:
(a) General requirements. The Secretary shall, pursuant to section 107(f)
of the Act, establish and supervise programs for the education and
training of employers and employees in the recognition, avoidance and
prevention of unsafe conditions in employments covered by the act.
(b) Employer responsibility.
(1) The employer should avail himself of the safety and health
training programs the Secretary provides.
(2) The employer shall instruct each employee in the recognition and
avoidance of unsafe conditions and the regulations applicable
to his work environment to control or eliminate any hazards or
other exposure to illness or injury.
(3) Employees required to handle or use poisons, caustics, and
other harmful substances shall be instructed regarding the safe
handling and use, and be made aware of the potential hazards,
personal hygiene, and personal protective measures required.
(4) In job site areas where harmful plants or animals are present,
employees who may be exposed shall be instructed regarding
the potential hazards, and how to avoid injury, and the first aid
procedures to be used in the event of injury.
(5) Employees required to handle or use flammable liquids, gases, or
toxic materials shall be instructed in the safe handling and use
of these materials and made aware of the specific requirements
contained in subparts D, F, and other applicable subparts of this part.
(6) (i)

A
 ll employees required to enter into confined or enclosed
spaces shall be instructed as to the nature of the hazards
involved, the necessary precautions to be taken, and in the
use of protective and emergency equipment required. The
employer shall comply with any specific regulations that
apply to work in dangerous or potentially dangerous areas.

 Construction

(ii) For purposes of paragraph (b)(6)(i) of this section, confined
or enclosed space means any space having a limited means
of egress, which is subject to the accumulation of toxic
or flammable contaminants or has an oxygen deficient
atmosphere. Confined or enclosed spaces include, but are
not limited to, storage tanks, process vessels, bins, boilers,
ventilation or exhaust ducts, sewers, underground utility
vaults, tunnels, pipelines, and open top spaces more than
4 feet in depth such as pits, tubs, vaults, and vessels.

title: Job Safety Analysis (JSA/JHA) & Hazard Identification Program
applicability: All contractors. A written process for identifying task hazards and controls before work.
required_elements: Written procedure to break jobs into steps, identify the hazard of each step, and define controls
Use of the hierarchy of controls (elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE)

(B) Retraining shall also be conducted whenever a

(D) The proper use of the special precautionary techniques,
personal protective equipment, insulating and shielding
materials, and insulated tools for working on or near
exposed energized parts of electric equipment.
Note: For the purposes of this section, a person
must have this training in order to be considered a
qualified person.
(iii) The employer shall determine, through regular supervision
and through inspections conducted on at least an annual
basis, that each employee is complying with the safetyrelated work practices required by this section.
(iv) An employee shall receive additional training (or
retraining) under any of the following conditions:
(A) If the supervision and annual inspections required
by paragraph (a)(2)(iii) of this section indicate that
the employee is not complying with the safety-related
work practices required by this section, or

74 

 Training Requirements

(B) If new technology, new types of equipment, or changes
in procedures necessitate the use of safety-related
work practices that are different from those which the
employee would normally use, or
(C) If he or she must employ safety-related work practices
that are not normally used during his or her regular
job duties.
Note: OSHA would consider tasks that are performed
less often than once per year to necessitate retraining
before the performance of the work practices involved.
(v) The training required by paragraph (a)(2) of this section
shall be of the classroom or on-the-job type.
(vi) The training shall establish employee proficiency in the
work practices required by this section and shall introduce
the procedures necessary for compliance with this section.
(vii) The employer shall certify that each employee has received
the training required by paragraph (a)(2) of this section. This
certification shall be made when the employee demonstrates
proficiency in the work practices involved and shall be
maintained for the duration of the employee’s employment.
Note: Employment records that indicate that an employee
has received the required training are an acceptable means
of meeting this requirement.
(b) Medical services and first aid. The employer shall provide medical
services and first aid as required in Section 1910.151 of this part. In
addition to the requirements of Section 1910.151 of this part, the
following requirements also apply:
(1) Cardiopulmonary resuscitation and first-aid training. When
employees are performing work on or associated with exposed
lines or equipment energized at 50 volts or more, persons trained
in first-aid including cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) shall
be available as follows:
(i)

For field work involving two or more employees at a work
location, at least two trained persons shall be available.
However, only one trained person need be available if all
new employees are trained in first aid, including CPR,
within 3 months of their hiring dates.

 General Industry

(ii) For fixed work locations such as generating stations, the
number of trained persons available shall be sufficient to
ensure that each employee exposed to electric shock can
be reached within 4 minutes by a trained person. However,
where the existing number of employees is insufficient to
meet this requirement (at a remote substation, for example),
all employees at the work location shall be trained.
(d) Hazardous energy control (lockout/tagout) procedures
(2) General.
(vi) The employer shall provide training to ensure that the
purpose and function of the energy control program are
understood by employees and that the knowledge and
skills required for the safe application, usage, and removal
of energy controls are acquired by employees. The training
shall include the following:
(A) Each authorized employee shall receive training in the
recognition of applicable hazardous energy sources,
the type and magnitude of energy available in the
workplace, and in the methods and means necessary
for energy isolation and control.
(B) Each affected employee shall be instructed in the
purpose and use of the energy control procedure.
(C) All other employees whose work operations are or
may be in an area where energy control procedures
may be used shall be instructed about the procedures
and about the prohibition relating to attempts to
restart or reenergize machines or equipment that are
locked out or tagged out.
(vii) When tagout systems are used, employees shall also be
trained in the limitation of tags.
(viii) Retraining shall be provided by the employer as follows:
(A) Retraining shall be provided for all authorized and
affected employees whenever there is a change in their
job assignments, a change in machines, equipment, or
processes that present a new hazard or whenever there
is a change in the energy control procedures.

76 

 Training Requirements

(B) Retraining shall also be conducted whenever a
periodic inspection under paragraph (d)(2)(v)
of this section reveals, or whenever the employer
has reason to believe, there are deviations from or
inadequacies in an employee’s knowledge or use of
the energy control procedures.
(C) The retraining shall reestablish employee proficiency
and shall introduce new or revised control methods
and procedures, as necessary.

Procedures shall be developed, documented and utilized for
the control of potentially hazardous energy when employees

Note: Exception: The employer need not document the

energy or reaccumulation of stored energy after shut

or equipment has a single energy source which can be
readily identified and isolated; (3) the isolation and locking

deactivate the machine or equipment; (4) the machine or
equipment is isolated from that energy source and locked

device will achieve a locked-out condition; (6) the lockout
device is under the exclusive control of the authorized

52

employee performing the servicing or maintenance; (7) the
servicing or maintenance does not create hazards for other
employees; and (8) the employer, in utilizing this exception,
has had no accidents involving the unexpected activation
or reenergization of the machine or equipment during
servicing or maintenance.
(6) Periodic Inspection.
(i)

The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the
energy control procedure at least annually to ensure that
the procedure and the requirements of this standard are
being followed.
(D) Where tagout is used for energy control, the periodic
inspection shall include a review, between the
inspector and each authorized and affected employee,
of that employee’s responsibilities under the energy
control procedure being inspected, and the elements
set forth in paragraph (c)(7)(ii) of this section.

(7) Training and communication.
(i)

The employer shall provide training to ensure that the
purpose and function of the energy control program are
understood by employees and that the knowledge and
skills required for the safe application, usage, and removal
of energy controls are acquired by employees. The training
shall include the following:
(A) Each authorized employee shall receive training in the
recognition of applicable hazardous energy sources,
the type and magnitude of the energy available in the
workplace, and the methods and means necessary for
energy isolation and control.
(B) Each affected employee shall be instructed in the
purpose and use of the energy control procedure.
(C) All other employees whose work operations are or
may be in an area where energy control procedures
may be utilized, shall be instructed about the
procedure, and about the prohibition relating
to attempts to restart or reenergize machines or
equipment which are locked out or tagged out.

(ii) When tagout systems are used, employees shall also be
trained in the following limitations of tags:

 General Industry

(A) Tags are essentially warning devices affixed to energy
isolating devices, and do not provide the physical
restraint on those devices that is provided by a lock.
(B) When a tag is attached to an energy isolating means,
it is not to be removed without authorization of the
authorized person for it, and it is never to be bypassed,
ignored, or otherwise defeated.
(C) Tags must be legible and understandable by all
authorized employees, affected employees, and all
other employees whose work operations are or may be
in the area, in order to be effective.
(D) Tags and their means of attachment must be made
of materials which will withstand the environmental
conditions encountered in the workplace.
(E) Tags may evoke a false sense of security, and their
meaning needs to be understood as part of the overall
energy control program.
(F) Tags must be securely attached to energy isolating
devices so that they cannot be inadvertently or
accidentally detached during use.
(iii) Employee retraining
(A) Retraining shall be provided for all authorized and
affected employees whenever there is a change in their
job assignments, a change in machines, equipment or
processes that present a new hazard, or when there is a
change in the energy control procedures.
(B) Additional retraining shall also be conducted
whenever a periodic inspection under paragraph (c)
(6) of this section reveals, or whenever the employer
has reason to believe, that there are deviations from
or inadequacies in the knowledge or use of the energy
control procedures.
(C) The retraining shall reestablish employee proficiency
and introduce new or revised control methods and
procedures, as necessary.
(iv) The employer shall certify that employee training has been
accomplished and is being kept up to date. The certification
shall contain each employee’s name and dates of training.

54 

 Training Requirements

(3): When the authorized employee who applied the lockout

(2) Outside Personnel (contractors, etc.)
(i)

Whenever outside servicing personnel are to be engaged

tagout procedures.

Prohibition on removing machine guards and on hands-in-line-of-fire practices
Impact-glove requirements where struck/pinch hazards exist
Injury-trend review focused on hand/finger incidents

(1) Employers shall provide employees with effective information

Workers under suspended loads

title: Housekeeping & Material Storage Program
applicability: All worksites; poor housekeeping is a common audit finding and a driver of slips/trips and fire hazards.

Safe material storage: stable stacking, height limits, aisle/egress clearance, and load ratings
Regular removal of scrap, waste, and combustibles; container/labeling requirements
Trip-hazard and spill control procedures
Housekeeping inspections and accountability
training: Workers trained on housekeeping standards and safe storage/stacking.
recordkeeping: Retain housekeeping inspection records.
failure_points: Blocked egress/aisles
Unstable/over-height storage
Accumulated combustibles

title: Confined and Enclosed Spaces — Shipyard (Competent Person / Marine Chemist)
applicability: Shipyard employment — ship repair, shipbuilding, shipbreaking, and related work in confined or enclosed spaces aboard vessels or in landside structures.
required_elements: Designation of a Competent Person to test and inspect confined/enclosed spaces before and during entry
Marine Chemist or Certified Industrial Hygiene certificate ('Safe for Workers'/'Safe for Hot Work') where required
Atmospheric testing for oxygen, flammable vapors (LEL), and toxic contaminants before entry and periodically
Labeling/posting of space status and controls to prevent unauthorized entry
Ventilation and continuous monitoring procedures for spaces immediately dangerous to life or health (IDLH)
Rescue and emergency procedures with equipment and trained standby personnel
training: Competent Person training; employee training on space hazards, testing results, PPE, and rescue. Retraining when conditions change.
recordkeeping: Retain Competent Person test records and Marine Chemist certificates for the duration of the job/shift as required by 1915.7.
failure_points: No designated Competent Person or Marine Chemist certificate for hot work
Atmospheric testing not repeated as conditions change
Rescue plan not space-specific or standby not equipped

title: Fire Protection in Shipyard Employment
applicability: All shipyard employment — establishes the fire safety program for ship repair, shipbuilding, and shipbreaking, including hot work and fire watch requirements.
required_elements: Written Fire Safety Plan per 1915.502: responsibilities, hot work permits, fire watch, alarm/notification, evacuation, and coordination with the fire response organization
Designation of a Fire Watch and their duties during and after hot work
Hot work authorization and control by a Competent Person
Fire response organization (in-house brigade or outside department) with defined capabilities
Employee alarm and notification system and evacuation procedures
Inspection and maintenance of fire detection, alarm, and suppression equipment
training: Training for fire watches, hot work operators, and members of the fire response organization; annual review.
recordkeeping: Retain the written fire safety plan, hot work permits, and fire watch/inspection records.
failure_points: No written fire safety plan or fire response organization identified
Fire watch not posted or not maintained 30 minutes after hot work
Hot work not authorized by a Competent Person

title: Personal Protective Equipment — Shipyard Employment
applicability: Shipyard employment where employees are exposed to hazards requiring PPE, including fall protection, respiratory protection, and personal fall arrest in shipyards.
required_elements: Written hazard assessment certifying the PPE required for each task
Selection, provision, and maintenance of head, eye, face, foot, hand, and body protection
Personal fall arrest and positioning systems where required (1915.159/.160)
Employer-provided PPE at no cost, with fit and condition verified
Employee training on use, limitations, care, and disposal of PPE
training: Training so each employee knows when PPE is necessary, what type, how to don/doff, limitations, and proper care.
recordkeeping: Retain the written PPE hazard-assessment certification and training records.
failure_points: No written hazard assessment certification
Fall protection not provided for shipyard elevations
PPE not provided at no cost or not maintained

with two energized conductors will also cause electric

title: Logging Operations
applicability: All logging operations regardless of end use of the wood — felling, bucking, limbing, yarding, loading, and transport of trees/logs.
required_elements: First-aid and CPR training for each employee, with first-aid kits at the worksite and each vehicle
PPE: head, eye, leg (chain-saw chaps), foot (cut-resistant), and hand protection provided at no cost
Chain saw and machine operation safe practices, inspection, and maintenance
Safe work procedures for felling, limbing, bucking, and manual/mechanical yarding
Signaling and communication among crew; safe distances (two-tree-length rule)
Danger-tree and environmental hazard evaluation before work begins
training: Initial and as-needed training on safe operation of each machine/tool; first-aid/CPR current; documented competency before solo work.
recordkeeping: Retain training certifications and first-aid/CPR records.

Chain-saw chaps/PPE not provided
Untrained employees felling timber
training_verbatim:
(i)(1) through (10)

(i) Training
(1) The employer shall provide training for each employee, including
supervisors, at no cost to the employee.
(2) Frequency. Training shall be provided as follows:
(i)

As soon as possible but not later than the effective date of this
section for initial training for each current and new employee;

(ii) Prior to initial assignment for each new employee;
(iii) Whenever the employee is assigned new work tasks, tools,
equipment, machines, or vehicles; and,
(iv) Whenever an employee demonstrates unsafe job performance.
(3) Content. At a minimum, training shall consist of the
following elements:
(i)

Safe performance of assigned work tasks;

(ii) Safe use, operation, and maintenance of tools,
machines, and vehicles the employee uses or operates,
including emphasis on understanding and following the
manufacturer’s operating and maintenance instructions,
warnings, and precautions;

68 

 Training Requirements

(iii) Recognition of safety and health hazards associated with the
employee’s specific work tasks, including the use of measures
and work practices to prevent or control those hazards;
(iv) Recognition, prevention, and control of other safety and
health hazards in the logging industry;
(v) Procedures, practices, and requirements of the employer’s
work site; and
(vi) The requirements of this standard.
(4) Training of an employee due to unsafe job performance, or
assignment of new work tasks, tools, equipment, machines, or
vehicles may be limited to those elements in paragraph (i)(3) of
this section which are relevant to the circumstances giving rise to
the need for training.
(5) Portability of training.
(i)

Each current employee who has received training in the
particular elements specified in paragraph (i)(3) of this
section shall not be required to be retrained in those elements.

(ii) Each new employee who has received training in the
particular elements specified in paragraph (i)(3) of this
section shall not be required to be retrained in those
elements prior to initial assignment.
(iii) The employer shall train each current and new employee
in those elements for which the employee has not received
training.
(iv) The employer is responsible for ensuring that each current
and new employee can properly and safely perform the
work tasks and operate the tools, equipment, machines, and
vehicles used in their job.
(6) Each new employee and each employee who is required to be
trained as specified in paragraph (i)(2) of this section, shall
work under the close supervision of a designated person until
the employee demonstrates to the employer the ability to safely
perform the new duties independently.
(7) First-aid training.
(i)

The employer shall assure that each employee, including
supervisors, receives or has received first-aid and CPR training
meeting at least the requirements specified in Appendix B.

 General Industry

(ii) The employer shall assure that each employee receives
first-aid training at least every three years and receives CPR
training at least annually.
(iii) The employer shall assure that each employee’s first-aid and
CPR training and/or certificate of training remain current.
(8) All training shall be conducted by a designated person.
(9) The employer shall assure that all training required by this
section is presented in a manner that the employee is able
to understand. The employer shall assure that all training
materials used are appropriate in content and vocabulary to the
educational level, literacy, and language skills of the employees
being trained.
(10) Certification of training.
(i)

The employer shall verify compliance with paragraph (i)
of this section by preparing a written certification record.
The written certification record shall contain the name or
other identity of the employee trained, the date(s) of the
training, and the signature of the person who conducted the
training or the signature of the employer. If the employer
relies on training conducted prior to the employee’s hiring
or completed prior to the effective date of this section, the
certification record shall indicate the date the employer
determined the prior training was adequate.

(ii) The most recent training certification shall be maintained.

or explosion, i.e., fuel (such as grain dust), oxygen, ignition source, and (in the case of
explosions) confinement. Employees should be made aware that any efforts they make to
keep these factors from occurring simultaneously will be an important step in reducing
the potential for fires and explosions.
The standard provides flexibility for the employer to design a training program which
fulfills the needs of a facility. The type, amount, and frequency of training will need
to reflect the tasks that employees are expected to perform. Although training is to
be provided to employees at least annually, it is recommended that safety meetings or
discussions and drills be conducted at more frequent intervals.
The training program should include those topics applicable to the particular facility,
as well as topics such as: Hot work procedures; lock-out/tag-out procedures; bin entry
procedures; bin cleaning procedures; grain dust explosions; fire prevention; procedures for
handling “hot grain”; housekeeping procedures, including methods and frequency of dust
removal; pesticide and fumigant usage; proper use and maintenance of personal protective
equipment; and, preventive maintenance. The types of work clothing should also be
considered in the program at least to caution against using polyester clothing that easily
melts and increases the severity of burns, as compared to wool or fire retardant cotton.
In implementing the training program, it is recommended that the employer utilize
films, slide-tape presentations, pamphlets, and other information which can be obtained
from such sources as the Grain Elevator and Processing Society, the Cooperative
Extension Service of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Kansas State University’s
Extension Grain Science and Industry, and other state agriculture schools, industry
associations, union organizations, and insurance groups.

(a) Scope. The training requirements contained in this section apply
to employees who face a risk of electric shock that is not reduced to
a safe level by the electrical installation requirements of 1910.303
through 1910.308.
Note: Employees in occupations listed in Table S-4 face such a risk
and are required to be trained. Other employees who also may
reasonably be expected to face comparable risk of injury due to
electric shock or other electrical hazards must also be trained.
(b) Content of training
(1) Practices addressed in this standard. Employees shall be trained
in and familiar with the safety-related work practices required by
1910.331 through 1910.335 that pertain to their respective job
assignments.
(2) Additional requirements for unqualified persons. Employees who
are covered by paragraph (a) of this section but who are not
qualified persons shall also be trained in and familiar with any
electrically related safety practices not specifically addressed by
1910.331 through 1910.335 but which are necessary for their
safety.
(3) Additional requirements for qualified persons. Qualified persons
(i.e., those permitted to work on or near exposed energized
parts) shall, at a minimum, be trained in and familiar with the
following:
(i)

The skills and techniques necessary to distinguish exposed
live parts from other parts of electric equipment.

(ii) The skills and techniques necessary to determine the
nominal voltage of exposed live parts, and
(iii) The clearance distances specified in 1910.333(c) and the
corresponding voltages to which the qualified person will
be exposed.
Note 1: For the purposes of 1910.331 through 1910.335, a
person must have the training required by paragraph (b)(3)
of this section in order to be considered a qualified person.

 General Industry

Note 2: Qualified persons whose work on energized
equipment involves either direct contact or contact by
means of tools or materials must also have the training
needed to meet 1910.333(C)(2).

classroom or on-the-job type. The degree of training provided shall be

employee performing the servicing or maintenance; (7) the

has had no accidents involving the unexpected activation
or reenergization of the machine or equipment during

(6) Periodic Inspection.
(i)

The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the
energy control procedure at least annually to ensure that
the procedure and the requirements of this standard are
being followed.
(D) Where tagout is used for energy control, the periodic
inspection shall include a review, between the
inspector and each authorized and affected employee,
of that employee’s responsibilities under the energy
control procedure being inspected, and the elements
set forth in paragraph (c)(7)(ii) of this section.

(7) Training and communication.
(i)

The employer shall provide training to ensure that the
purpose and function of the energy control program are
understood by employees and that the knowledge and
skills required for the safe application, usage, and removal
of energy controls are acquired by employees. The training
shall include the following:
(A) Each authorized employee shall receive training in the
recognition of applicable hazardous energy sources,
the type and magnitude of the energy available in the
workplace, and the methods and means necessary for
energy isolation and control.
(B) Each affected employee shall be instructed in the
purpose and use of the energy control procedure.
(C) All other employees whose work operations are or
may be in an area where energy control procedures
may be utilized, shall be instructed about the
procedure, and about the prohibition relating
to attempts to restart or reenergize machines or
equipment which are locked out or tagged out.

(ii) When tagout systems are used, employees shall also be
trained in the following limitations of tags:

 General Industry

(A) Tags are essentially warning devices affixed to energy
isolating devices, and do not provide the physical
restraint on those devices that is provided by a lock.
(B) When a tag is attached to an energy isolating means,
it is not to be removed without authorization of the
authorized person for it, and it is never to be bypassed,
ignored, or otherwise defeated.
(C) Tags must be legible and understandable by all
authorized employees, affected employees, and all
other employees whose work operations are or may be
in the area, in order to be effective.
(D) Tags and their means of attachment must be made
of materials which will withstand the environmental
conditions encountered in the workplace.
(E) Tags may evoke a false sense of security, and their
meaning needs to be understood as part of the overall
energy control program.
(F) Tags must be securely attached to energy isolating
devices so that they cannot be inadvertently or
accidentally detached during use.
(iii) Employee retraining
(A) Retraining shall be provided for all authorized and
affected employees whenever there is a change in their
job assignments, a change in machines, equipment or
processes that present a new hazard, or when there is a
change in the energy control procedures.
(B) Additional retraining shall also be conducted
whenever a periodic inspection under paragraph (c)
(6) of this section reveals, or whenever the employer
has reason to believe, that there are deviations from
or inadequacies in the knowledge or use of the energy
control procedures.
(C) The retraining shall reestablish employee proficiency
and introduce new or revised control methods and
procedures, as necessary.
(iv) The employer shall certify that employee training has been
accomplished and is being kept up to date. The certification

title: Shock Risk Assessment and Approach Boundaries
applicability: Performed whenever an employee may be exposed to an energized part at 50 V or more. Determines how close a person may approach and what shock PPE is required.
required_elements: Identify the nominal system voltage of the exposed part
Determine the limited approach boundary (the distance beyond which an unqualified person must not cross without a qualified escort and PPE)
Determine the restricted approach boundary (only a qualified person, with a documented plan and shock PPE, may cross)
Select shock PPE: rubber insulating gloves (with leather protectors) and insulated/insulating tools rated for the voltage
Estimate the likelihood and severity of a shock and apply controls
training: Qualified persons trained to look up the correct boundaries for the voltage and to don voltage-rated gloves and use insulated tools.
recordkeeping: Glove test records (retest cycle typically 6 months); tool inspection records.
failure_points: Using the wrong voltage class of gloves
No restricted approach boundary observed while reaching into a live panel
Untested / expired rubber insulating gloves
source: https://www.osha.gov/electrical  (NFPA 70E is the consensus arc-flash method OSHA references; buy the standard at nfpa.org/70E)
notes: Exact boundary distances live in NFPA 70E Table 130.4(E)(a)/(b) by voltage — Origin cites the table and voltage but does not reproduce the copyrighted distance values. Look them up in the current 70E.

title: Arc-Flash Risk Assessment and Incident-Energy Analysis
applicability: Required before working within the arc-flash boundary on energized equipment, or when the equipment condition (doors open, covers off) exposes an arc-flash hazard.
required_elements: Determine the arc-flash boundary — the distance at which incident energy equals 1.2 cal/cm2 (the onset of a second-degree burn)

Choose ONE method and do not mix them on a task: (a) incident-energy analysis — calculate incident energy in cal/cm2 (commonly via IEEE 1584 / an engineering study) and select AR PPE with an arc rating at or above it; or (b) the PPE-category (table) method in 70E 130.7(C)(15)
Account for equipment condition and maintenance (an un-maintained breaker that fails to clear raises incident energy)
Reflect results on the equipment arc-flash label and keep the study current (re-study when the electrical system changes)
training: Persons performing the analysis are qualified/competent in the method used; field workers are trained to read the label and select PPE accordingly.
recordkeeping: The arc-flash / incident-energy study, the label schedule, and the re-study trigger log.
failure_points: No incident-energy study and no PPE-category basis — boundaries are guessed
Study never updated after transformer/breaker/utility changes
Mixing the two methods on the same task
source: https://www.osha.gov/electrical  (NFPA 70E is the consensus arc-flash method OSHA references; buy the standard at nfpa.org/70E)
notes: 1.2 cal/cm2 (second-degree-burn threshold) is a published scientific value and is stated as such. The PPE-category selection tables (130.7(C)(15)) are copyrighted 70E content — cite them, do not reproduce.

title: Arc-Rated PPE and Insulated Tool Selection
applicability: Applies whenever an employee works inside the arc-flash boundary or where a shock hazard exists.
required_elements: Select arc-rated (AR) clothing and equipment with an arc rating (ATPV or EBT, in cal/cm2) at or above the assessed incident energy — or the PPE ensemble specified by the chosen PPE category

Cover the arc-flash hazard body zones: AR shirt/pants or coverall, AR face shield with balaclava or an arc-flash hood, hard hat, safety glasses, hearing protection, and heavy-duty leather (or AR) gloves
Rubber insulating gloves with leather protectors, rated for the system voltage, for shock protection
No meltable synthetic fabrics (nylon, polyester, acetate) as underlayers next to skin
Inspect PPE before use; keep AR garments clean and un-modified (repairs must preserve arc rating)
training: Workers trained to read the label/PPE category and don the correct ensemble; trained on inspection and care.
recordkeeping: Rubber-goods (glove/sleeve) electrical test records; PPE inspection log.
failure_points: AR clothing rating below the incident energy at the task
Meltable synthetics worn under AR clothing
Voltage-rated gloves used without leather protectors or past test date
source: https://www.osha.gov/electrical  (NFPA 70E is the consensus arc-flash method OSHA references; buy the standard at nfpa.org/70E)
notes: Exact PPE ensembles per category are in NFPA 70E Table 130.7(C)(15) — cite, do not copy.

title: Energized Electrical Work Permit (EEWP)
applicability: Required when work will be performed on or near exposed energized parts inside the restricted approach boundary or the arc-flash boundary and the equipment is NOT placed in an electrically safe work condition.
required_elements: A written permit that describes the circuit/equipment and the specific work
Justification why de-energizing is infeasible or introduces a greater hazard (energized work is only allowed on these two grounds)
The shock and arc-flash risk assessment results: boundaries and required PPE
Safe work practices, the means to restrict unqualified access, and evidence of a job briefing
Authorized-approval signatures (a level of management above the worker) before work begins
Defined exemptions: testing, troubleshooting, and voltage measurement by a qualified person in appropriate PPE do not require a written EEWP but still require the risk assessment and PPE
training: Qualified persons and the approving manager trained on when a permit is required and how to complete it.
recordkeeping: Retain completed EEWPs (commonly per project or a fixed retention term) as proof energized work was justified and controlled.
failure_points: Energized work performed with no permit and no infeasibility justification
Permit signed by the worker only (no independent management authorization)
Treating routine energized tasks as exempt without doing the risk assessment
source: https://www.osha.gov/electrical  (NFPA 70E is the consensus arc-flash method OSHA references; buy the standard at nfpa.org/70E)
notes: Origin ships a fillable EEWP form template. The 'infeasible or greater hazard' test is the crux reviewers check — production convenience is not a valid justification.

title: Arc-Flash Equipment Labeling
applicability: Applies to switchboards, panelboards, industrial control panels, meter socket enclosures, and motor control centers in other than dwelling units that are likely to require examination, adjustment, servicing, or maintenance while energized.
required_elements: Field-marked label on the equipment showing nominal system voltage
The arc-flash boundary
At least one of: available incident energy and the corresponding working distance, OR the minimum arc rating of clothing, OR the required PPE category (one method, consistent with the study)
Labels legible, durable, and updated when the study changes

recordkeeping: Label schedule tied to the arc-flash study; re-label log when the system changes.
failure_points: Unlabeled gear that is serviced energized
Label data inconsistent with the current study
notes: The label duty is OSHA-enforceable via 1910.303 design requirements plus the general duty clause; 70E 130.5(H) specifies the content.

title: Qualified vs. Unqualified Person — Electrical Training
applicability: Defines who may do electrical work and what training each class needs. Prequal reviewers routinely ask for the qualified-person roster and training records.
required_elements: Definition of a qualified person: trained and demonstrably able to identify and avoid the electrical hazards, determine nominal voltage, use PPE and insulated tools, and apply approach boundaries — qualification is task- and equipment-specific
Definition of an unqualified person and the limits on their exposure (must stay outside the limited approach boundary unless escorted and protected)
Training content: safety-related work practices, ESWC/LOTO, boundaries, arc-flash, PPE, and emergency response including release/resuscitation
Retraining at least every 3 years, and when new equipment/procedures are introduced, when practices are not followed, or when an audit finds a deficiency
Documentation of each employee, the training content, the date, and demonstrated proficiency
training: Delivered by a competent instructor; proficiency demonstrated, not just attended.
recordkeeping: Qualified-person roster; training records with content, date, trainer, and retrain-due dates.
failure_points: Calling someone 'qualified' with no documented training or demonstrated skill
Training older than the 3-year retrain cycle
No emergency-response / CPR component for those exposed to shock hazards
notes: Qualification is not a blanket title — a person can be qualified on one system/task and unqualified on another.

title: Determining Work-Relatedness (and the Exceptions)
applicability: The first gate before any case is recorded. A case is work-related if an event or exposure in the work environment caused or contributed to the condition, or significantly aggravated a pre-existing condition.
required_elements: Apply the presumption: injuries/illnesses arising from the work environment are presumed work-related unless a listed exception applies

Know the exceptions (1904.5(b)(2)): e.g., present as a member of the public; symptoms surface at work but result solely from a non-work event; voluntary wellness/health-club activity; eating/drinking own food; personal grooming/self-medication for a non-work condition; common cold or flu; certain mental illness cases without a professional opinion linking to work
Handle travel-status and work-at-home cases per the special rules in 1904.5(b)(6)-(7)
Decide 'new case' vs. continuation of an old case under 1904.6
recordkeeping: Document the basis for any not-work-related determination in case of an audit.
failure_points: Recording (or not recording) without applying the 1904.5(b)(2) exceptions
Treating a recurrence of an old injury as a new case
notes: Work-relatedness errors are a top driver of a wrong TRIR — both over- and under-recording distort a prequal score.

title: General Recording Criteria — Is the Case Recordable?
applicability: Once a case is work-related and a new case, 1904.7 decides recordability. This is the decision the entire TRIR/DART calculation rests on.
required_elements: Record if the case results in ANY of: death; days away from work; restricted work or transfer to another job; medical treatment beyond first aid; loss of consciousness; or a significant injury/illness diagnosed by a physician or other licensed health care professional
Use the closed 'first aid' list in 1904.7(b)(5)(ii) — anything NOT on that list is 'medical treatment beyond first aid' and is recordable (e.g., prescription meds, sutures, rigid splints)
Count calendar days (not workdays) for days-away and restricted/transfer; begin counting the day AFTER the injury; cap the total at 180 days
If a case moves from restricted to days-away, update the classification to the more serious outcome
Special recording criteria (1904.8-.12): needlesticks/sharps, medical removal, hearing loss (STS + 25 dB), TB, and (where in effect) MSDs
recordkeeping: Record within 7 calendar days of learning of the case; keep the 300 Log current.
failure_points: Misclassifying prescription medication or sutures as 'first aid' (they are recordable)
Counting workdays instead of calendar days
Not capping days at 180
notes: The single most important record in the KB for TRIR accuracy. When in doubt, the first-aid list is exhaustive — if a treatment is not on it, it is recordable.

title: OSHA 300 Log, 301 Report, and Privacy Concern Cases
applicability: Governs the forms themselves: what goes on the 300 Log, the 301 Incident Report, and how to protect employee privacy for sensitive cases.
required_elements: Maintain an OSHA 300 Log (or equivalent) for each establishment expected to be in operation for a year or more; enter each recordable case within 7 days
Complete an OSHA 301 Incident Report (or equivalent such as a workers' comp first report) for each recordable case within 7 days

Privacy concern cases — do NOT enter the employee's name on the 300 Log; write 'privacy case' and keep a separate confidential list: injuries to intimate body parts/reproductive system, sexual assaults, mental illnesses, HIV/hepatitis/TB, needlesticks/sharps involving contamination, and any case where the employee voluntarily requests name omission
Give employees and former employees access to their own records on request (1904.35)
recordkeeping: Keep the separate privacy-case list secure; provide records to employees/reps per 1904.35 and to government per 1904.40.
failure_points: Employee name shown on a privacy-concern case
301 (or equivalent) not completed within 7 days
notes: A separate confidential list is mandatory for privacy cases — a 300 Log that names them is a recordkeeping violation.

title: OSHA 300A Annual Summary — Certification and Posting
applicability: The year-end obligation. Required even for an establishment with zero recordable cases (post the form showing zeros).
required_elements: At year end, review the 300 Log for completeness and accuracy and correct any deficiencies
Total the columns and enter them on the OSHA 300A Annual Summary, including average employees and total hours worked

Certify the summary: a company executive (owner/officer, highest-ranking company official at the site, or that person's immediate supervisor) signs certifying the log was examined and the summary is correct
Post the certified 300A in a conspicuous place from February 1 through April 30 of the year following the year covered
Post even if there were zero recordable cases
recordkeeping: Retain the certified 300A for 5 years; keep the certifier's signature.
failure_points: 300A certified by a safety manager/HR clerk instead of a company executive
Posted late, removed early, or not posted because there were zero cases
Hours worked or average employees left blank (breaks TRIR calculation)
notes: 'Company executive' is defined narrowly in 1904.32(b)(4) — the most common recordkeeping citation and a frequent prequal rejection.

title: Reporting Fatalities and Severe Injuries to OSHA
applicability: Applies to ALL employers — including those otherwise partially exempt from recordkeeping. Separate from the 300 Log.
required_elements: Report a work-related fatality within 8 hours of learning of it
Report a work-related in-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye within 24 hours of learning of it
Report via the OSHA 800-number, the online reporting form, or the nearest area office
Fatality reportable if it occurs within 30 days of the incident; in-patient hospitalization/amputation/eye loss reportable if it occurs within 24 hours of the incident
Provide: establishment name, location/time of incident, type of event, number affected, names, and a contact
recordkeeping: Keep a record of the report made (date, time, who reported, confirmation).
failure_points: Missing the 8-hour (fatality) / 24-hour (hospitalization, amputation, eye) window
Assuming a partially exempt employer need not report (they must)
notes: An amputation includes fingertip amputations with bone loss. Late reporting is a distinct, separately citable violation.

title: Electronic Submission of Injury Data (ITA)
applicability: Determines which establishments must upload their injury data to OSHA's Injury Tracking Application (ITA) each year, and what they upload.
required_elements: Establishments with 250+ employees (in industries required to keep records) submit the 300A electronically
Establishments with 20-249 employees in designated higher-hazard industries (Appendix A to Subpart E) submit the 300A

Since the 2024 rule: establishments with 100+ employees in the highest-hazard industries (Appendix B) submit the 300 Log and 301 Incident Report data in addition to the 300A, including the establishment's legal company name
Annual deadline: March 2 for the prior calendar year
Submit through the ITA web portal (manual entry, CSV upload, or API)
recordkeeping: Retain the ITA submission confirmation; reconcile submitted totals to the posted 300A.
failure_points: Not knowing the establishment's industry falls in Appendix A/B
Missing the March 2 deadline
Counts submitted don't match the posted 300A
notes: Coverage is by establishment size and industry, not just company size. The 2024 rule expanded case-detail (300/301) submission for large high-hazard establishments.

title: Retention and Updating of Records
applicability: How long the forms are kept and the duty to keep them accurate during that window.
required_elements: Retain the OSHA 300 Log, the privacy-case list, the 300A Annual Summary, and the 301 Incident Reports for 5 years following the end of the calendar year those records cover
During the 5-year retention period, update the stored 300 Log to include newly discovered recordable cases and to reflect changes to recorded cases (the 300A does not have to be updated)
On business transfer, the receiving employer must retain the prior records for the remainder of the period
recordkeeping: Store all 5 years accessibly for employee access (1904.35) and government requests (1904.40, within 4 business hours).
failure_points: Discarding logs before the 5-year window
Not updating a prior-year 300 Log when a case later becomes recordable
notes: Government access requests under 1904.40 must be met within 4 business hours — retention alone is not enough; the records must be retrievable.

title: OSHA Injury & Illness Recordkeeping Program
applicability: A written program that documents HOW the company keeps its OSHA injury/illness records accurately and on time. Prequal platforms (ISN RAVS, Avetta, Veriforce, PEC) accept a recordkeeping procedure as evidence the TRIR/DART they grade is reliable.
required_elements: Assigned recordkeeper and backup, with authority and training
Work-relatedness and recordability decision procedure (1904.5 / 1904.7), including use of the first-aid list and day-counting rules
OSHA 300 Log and 301 Incident Report procedure — entered within 7 calendar days
Privacy-concern-case handling (separate confidential list; no name on the 300 Log)
OSHA 300A annual review, executive certification, and Feb 1-Apr 30 posting
Severe-injury reporting procedure (fatality 8 hr; hospitalization/amputation/eye 24 hr) with the reporting method and contacts
ITA electronic submission procedure and the March 2 deadline (if the establishment is covered)
5-year retention, updating during retention, and employee/government access
training: The recordkeeper (and backup) is trained on the 1904.5/.7 decision tree, the first-aid list, day counting, privacy cases, posting, reporting windows, and ITA submission.
recordkeeping: Retain 300, 300A, 301, and the privacy-case list for 5 years following the year covered; keep ITA confirmations and the reporting log.
failure_points: 300A not certified by a company executive
Recordability decisions inconsistent (drives a wrong TRIR)
Late severe-injury reporting
No named, trained recordkeeper
notes: This is the written-program companion to the 1904 reference records. Naming its template program-osha-recordkeeping-program.md auto-wires it to the gap-draft engine.
